Patient Vignette: Mr. A.

Mr. A. is a 67-year-old married man, a retired school principal, who presents for an initial consultation at the urging of his wife. He sits forward in his chair, hands clasped, his posture still carrying the authoritative ease of a man who spent decades managing a school building. He is articulate, but his voice has a new, hesitant quality, as if he is constantly checking his own words.

The event that changed everything happened eight months ago, on a clear Tuesday morning. Mr. A. was driving to a district meeting, a route he had taken hundreds of times. He remembers the sun, the taste of his coffee, the familiar rhythm of the road. Then, a large pick-up truck ran a red light at an intersection. He recalls the sound—a deafening, metallic scream of tearing metal. He remembers the violent spin, the world becoming a blur of shattered glass and deployed airbag dust. He was trapped in his car for twenty minutes, the smell of gasoline heavy in the air, convinced the engine would ignite. He thought of his wife, his daughters, the unfinished paperwork on his desk. He thought, This is how it ends.

Physically, he escaped with a broken wrist and bruised ribs. The physical wounds have healed. But Mr. A. has not left that intersection.

In the weeks following the accident, he could not drive. His wife drove him everywhere. He felt a deep, irrational shame watching her navigate the car, his hands trembling on his lap. He would see a truck in the rearview mirror and his heart would begin to pound, a cold sweat breaking on his brow. He started to avoid the intersection itself, taking a 15-minute detour through a residential area to get to the grocery store. He told himself it was just good sense.

The avoidance has since spread. He no longer drives on the highway. He has stopped attending the monthly retired principals’ luncheon because it is held across town. His world has shrunk. He spends most of his time in his home office, organizing his old files, a task he finds both pointless and compulsively necessary for the feeling of control it offers. Sleep is a battlefield. He is terrified of the dreams. He will jolt awake at 3:17 AM—the exact time the police report logged the accident—drenched in sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs, the sound of the crash echoing in the silence of his bedroom. He now sleeps in the guest room so as not to disturb his wife.

His wife, a retired teacher, has become his caretaker, a role she never asked for. He sees the worry in her eyes, the way she hesitates before asking him to run a simple errand. He feels a profound, crushing guilt. He is irritable, snapping at small things—a misplaced key, a phone call during dinner. He feels like a ghost in his own life. The man who once calmly mediated disputes between angry parents and frustrated teenagers now feels a raw, unmanageable panic in the produce aisle of the supermarket. He cannot concentrate on a book. He feels detached, as if a pane of glass has been placed between him and the world. He describes it as a constant, low-level hum of dread, a sense that the safe, predictable world he built for forty years was just a thin crust over a void.

He has not told his daughters about the extent of his struggle. He was always the rock, the problem-solver, the principal who had a plan for everything. Now, he feels like a problem with no solution. He is here today, he says, because his wife made the appointment. He is not sure it will help. He looks out the window, his jaw tight, and says quietly, "I just want to feel like myself again. I don't know where he went."
